query: Consider the following context: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) exhibit excellent properties such as high strength, good ductility, superior corrosion resistance, and thermal stability, making them highly promising for applications in the aerospace, energy, and automotive industries. Among them, the FeNiCrMn HEA demonstrates outstanding corrosion resistance while eliminating the expensive Co element present in the “Cantor” alloy, significantly reducing costs. However, current research on the FeNiCrMn HEA has primarily focused on its corrosion resistance, with relatively limited studies on its mechanical properties. In that context, which method can be used for the stated problem, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Processing the FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy via additive manufacturing (specifically selective laser melting) will enhance its mechanical properties relative to conventional processing by promoting a refined microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrMn HEA produced by conventional casting or wrought methods that exhibits excellent corrosion resistance but unoptimized mechanical properties.
generation.intervention: Use selective laser melting (SLM) to fabricate FeNiCrMn HEA samples.
generation.conditions: Optimized SLM parameters (e.g., linear energy density, laser scan speed) that induce rapid solidification under inert atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined grain structure and improved phase homogeneity achieved through the rapid cooling inherent in SLM.
generation.mechanism: The high cooling rates in SLM lead to a fine-grained microstructure and reduced segregation, which in turn should improve yield strength and ductility, while potential processing-induced defects (e.g., porosity) can be minimized by proper parameter optimization.
generation.predicted_outcome: SLM-processed FeNiCrMn HEA samples will demonstrate higher yield and tensile strengths as well as improved ductility compared to samples produced by conventional methods.
generation.baseline: Conventional processing routes for FeNiCrMn HEA where mechanical properties have not been systematically optimized.
generation.boundary: The improvements are subject to the SLM process quality; excessive porosity or residual stresses could counteract the benefits of the refined microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: Precise quantitative changes in mechanical properties are uncertain and depend on fine-tuning the SLM parameters; the balance between benefit from microstructural refinement and potential processing defects remains to be fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrMn HEA samples: one set via conventional processing (casting/wrought) and another set via optimized SLM. Conduct microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM) to quantify grain size and porosity, and perform standardized mechanical tests (tensile and compression tests) to assess yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SLM-fabricated FeNiCrMn HEA samples do not show statistically significant improvements in mechanical properties (e.g., higher yield strength and better ductility) over conventional samples, or if any improvements are negated by processing defects, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.

Abstract The growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material.
